code.caption: The official counter tutorial starts from a compiled Page. Identify the namespaces and Content tree; x:Class belongs to that project, not the runtime-XAML editor.
This official tutorial uses C# Markup construction. Compare object creation and property configuration with the plain-C# starter; the fluent helpers require their project packages.
Read the project SDK and feature declarations. Ellipses mark omitted project context; this is not a complete project file to paste unchanged.
Each attribute configures a property on a constructed TextBlock. Compare whitespace in the source with explicit layout properties.
The enclosing Page supplies project and namespace context. Compare this built-page example with the smaller StackPanel root accepted by the playground.
The constructor registers Click and GettingFocus handlers on named controls created by InitializeComponent. Notice the captured output control and the source objects holding the delegates.
The same sample pairs Loaded subscription with Unloaded unsubscription. Read both sides of the ownership boundary, not just the += line.

A UI-thread runtime test adds a second child, waits for relayout and checks height changes from 50 to 100. The helper class and test host remain in the enclosing file.
This adjustable Grid uses fixed child dimensions, Auto and star tracks, spacing bindings and spans. Compare these additional constraints with the simpler four-track equation in the atlas.
The sample’s controls expose spacing and show a Margin around the Grid. Distinguish the external Margin from ColumnSpacing and RowSpacing inside it.
Button and TextBlock styles deliberately supply different foreground values. The expected green text demonstrates style/inheritance context; it is not merely a global color variable.
A shared item template contains a named CheckBox and a binding to that row’s IsChecked. Each template instance has its own objects and context; the surrounding sample supplies the item collection.
The actual sample declares a width-driven adaptive state. Identify the trigger condition and setter target, then compare with the imperative SizeChanged starter.
The sample binds TextBoxes in TwoWay, OneWay and default modes to the same named property. Read its code-behind for the source object and compare directions before typing.
The official MVVM tutorial uses ObservableObject and generated ObservableProperty members. Compare those generated notifications with the manual INotifyPropertyChanged setter in the runnable lesson.
Changing binding mode changes allowed value flow, not persistence. The backing property and its notifications are defined in this sample’s paired code-behind.

ItemsSource refers to one ObservableCollection and the UI offers Add, Remove and Replace operations. A collection notification is different from a property change inside an item.
Replacement, removal and insertion mutate collection membership or identity. The helper methods depend on surrounding sample data and are not standalone functions.

The complete tutorial view-model fragment combines observable properties and a generated Increment command. This is project-generator code; the online starter demonstrates the validation rule directly.
Read state and action as one small view-model contract. The generator removes boilerplate but does not decide domain boundaries, persistence or validation policy.

The official example makes Countable state explicit and connects it to Uno reactive state. Compare the record transition with the ordinary immutable-record lab before adopting package-generated binding adapters.

A navigation collaborator enters through a view-model constructor. The surrounding migration guide defines the interface and command helper; inspect the replaceable dependency, not just the command syntax.
This short route-registration example shows an explicit singleton lifetime in the guide’s navigation context. It is not a complete hosting setup or a recommendation to make every service a singleton.
The destination reads a typed parameter during OnNavigatedTo. The parameter identifies state rather than passing a live visual tree.
Navigation and visual attachment have distinct callbacks. Read the comments and compare navigation lifetime with Loaded/Unloaded ownership.
The HTTP tutorial coordinates IsBusy with try/finally around loading. It does not pass cancellation in this fragment: identify that boundary and compare with the token-aware runnable lesson.

Actual ApplicationData file creation and read/write operations illustrate storage, distinct from JSON serialization. These APIs run under the host’s storage policy; the course iframe has only ephemeral settings.
This small settings example stores and reads a value. It demonstrates the API, not schema validation, encryption, quotas or a crash-safe multi-file transaction.

The tutorial checks HTTP status before reading successful content. Examine disposal, cancellation and error policy in the full application; the course starter replaces transport with a deterministic handler.
This launch-settings fragment supplies development addresses for the server host. It is public configuration, not a place to hide browser-client secrets or an entire appsettings contract.
The page uses resource identifiers on UI elements. Resource lookup translates text; CultureInfo formatting in the starter is a separate operation.
The code-behind obtains a resource string in the guide’s project context. Observe the key lookup and do not confuse it with automatic translation of arbitrary literals.

A provider-specific sign-in callback processes an OIDC response using initialized project fields. This is a contextual guide excerpt, not a standalone or universal login implementation; authorization still belongs to the trusted service.
The example records an error through the configured logging abstraction. Review what the error contains before logging it; never assume upstream error text cannot include sensitive data.
Uno exposes a log-level choice for not-implemented API diagnostics. A diagnostic category and severity are policies, not user-facing error recovery.
The feature list declares optional capabilities. Read it as an example of feature selection, not a prescription to install every listed feature for a small application.
This WinUI-style registration names the property, type, owner and metadata. The guide contrasts it with Xamarin.Forms; the excerpt is the Uno/WinUI side.
The runtime regression registers a property-changed callback, unregisters its token, changes the property and asserts no notification. Token ownership matters independently of the CLR wrapper.
The named Image part reads Source from the templated parent. The custom presenter class supplies the behavior; this resource dictionary alone is not a complete control.
This manual coordinate sample uses GetCurrentPoint(null). Compare that coordinate context with GetCurrentPoint(surface) in the starter; do not combine points from different spaces.
The sample assigns names to different visual elements. Inspect the actual resulting role, name and state; setting Name alone does not make an arbitrary Border an operable button.
The Uno/WinUI side declares a Storyboard and target property. Named targets and surrounding transforms belong to the enclosing XAML project; the isolated fragment is not a standalone root.
The named element owns a CompositeTransform and a Storyboard targets its translation. Compare timing, endpoints and transform ownership with the opacity starter.
This actual shapes/brushes example separates geometry elements from their brushes. Inspect the complete resource and layout context before adapting it.
The helper observes MeasureOverride and ArrangeOverride independently while delegating real work to the base class. Observation counts are not elapsed-time measurements.
The runtime test adds/removes a child, awaits relayout and checks both measured and arranged height. Those assertions connect the mutation to observable geometry.

The sample’s deterministic flow scrolls and modifies items above the viewport. It is a concrete scenario for inspecting container behavior and maintaining identity, not a universal fixed-height recycling algorithm.
The diagnostic example follows live-object lifetime. It is investigative code in a memory-troubleshooting guide, not a production cache implementation; compare it with the bounded cache model.
This guide fragment converts TryEnqueue into an awaitable completion with a TaskCompletionSource. Queue acceptance, execution and exception completion are distinct outcomes.
The sample updates text and awaits Task.Yield in a loop. Yielding creates a scheduling opportunity; it does not remove total work or prove a new frame is presented every iteration.
Collecting a trace by process ID is an actual tooling step. Replace PID with the intended target process and record workload/build context; this command is not executed by the browser lesson.
The guide shows a platform-specific trace collection route. Platform prerequisites and tool versions remain in the source; do not generalize one host’s trace to all renderers.
Publish the explicit browser target and inspect its generated assets. A successful command is followed by runtime and hosting checks.

This linker-descriptor fragment preserves dynamically used members in its example assembly. It illustrates why reflection needs explicit consideration, not a blanket instruction to disable all trimming.

The tutorial resets IsBusy in finally around data loading. That restores one invariant; separate error/cancelled/empty states and safe retry policy still need application design.
The documented publish command selects the browser artifact. A real delivery gate must then inspect, test and promote that exact output.

The tutorial view model is a compact state/action reference. Extend the capstone deliberately with stable IDs, draft validation and persistence rather than treating a generated counter as the finished task application.

These sample mutations show explicit insert/remove/replace operations and item construction. The capstone must preserve stable domain identity across projection and persistence; these positional helpers are not that complete design.
A short instrumentation helper makes the measure/arrange boundary visible. Follow its base calls in the source and compare with a runtime test before generalizing behavior.
The sample marker illustrates how repository examples are discovered. It identifies project context, not a complete standalone application.
The same template recipe contains a named CheckBox in every row instance. Read the ElementName binding as a scope-specific relationship, then compare with generated binding code.

This generated-binding excerpt explains implementation at the pinned source revision and includes its historical namespace form. Do not edit generated output or paste it into runtime XAML as a lasting fix.
The style/inheritance sample shows distinct foreground sources. It complements the live local-FontSize/ClearValue experiment; the two examples deliberately test different precedence relationships.

This proportional panel derives one dimension from the other and has target-specific branches. Its sizing policy differs from the lesson’s vertical stack: compare both MeasureOverride and ArrangeOverride rather than copying it as a generic panel.

The custom drawing element reacts to a Sample dependency-property change and calls Invalidate before RenderOverride draws. Its callback clamps a value; production callback designs should guard any recursive update. This does not implement the atlas’s tile classifier.
A concrete regression establishes setup, awaited state and expected geometry. Use this structure to design your own discriminating test; its UI-thread host is part of the contract.
This repository UI-test example selects a sample and inspects a result. Read neighboring assertions and helpers and do not confuse retry infrastructure with proof that a flaky application is correct.
